Subject: Dedicated pool onboarding — throughput headroom / temporary queuing

Hi Tessa,

Thanks again for the walkthrough this morning. We liked the Dedicated capacity proposal but wanted to flag one operational constraint on our side: during the first 72 hours of model rollout we'll be pushing a lot of concurrent small requests (spikey fanout from our inference orchestrator) as we validate edge cases.

Two quick questions:
- Can Redwood guarantee the committed throughput (tokens/sec) for the reserved GPUs when the pool is at 100% utilization?
- If we see brief spikes above the committed throughput, what's your standard behavior around queueing vs shedding traffic? Our SRE lead wants to know if we should expect increased latency (queueing) or dropped requests and whether that can be treated as an agreed temporary SLA variance during onboarding.

We're asking for a temporary exception (48–72 hours) to tolerate queueing up to ~2s added tail latency for small requests if that avoids request loss — we'd like to formalize that in the mutual action plan if possible. Procurement is copied for contract alignment.

I've attached a simple traffic sketch and our onboarding checklist.

From: lukas_meyer <lukas_meyer@redwood.ai>

Subject: Re: Dedicated pool onboarding — throughput headroom / temporary queuing

TL;DR: Reserved GPU pools commit to a steady-state throughput target (tokens/sec) per the configuration. For short spikes we have two configurable behaviors: queue (backpressure) or reject (429-style).

Details:
- Committed baseline: the pool will reserve N GPUs and we provision to meet the declared baseline throughput at 90th percentile for your observed request size distribution. That baseline is guaranteed unless the customer changes model/seq lengths drastically.
- Spike handling: by default our Dedicated runtime applies request queueing with a soft cap on queue depth; this preserves throughput but increases tail latency. We can set the soft cap such that the 95th->99th percentile tail adds no more than 1.5–2.5s for the small requests you described.
- Rejection policy: alternatively, we can apply aggressive shedding which returns quick errors under overload.
- Observability: we'll surface per-route queue depth and queue wait histograms in the Console and emit traces for any request with >500ms queue wait.

For your ask (48–72h onboarding window): we can take a temporary operational variance to accept queueing up to 2s of added tail latency (measured at the request ingress) provided we capture this in the MAP and you accept a shorter window for escalations. If queueing exceeds the bound, standard SLA credits would apply per the Dedicated terms.

Action items I recommend including in the MAP:
- Explicit onboarding window (start/end times).
- Targeted routes for the rollout (so we can apply route-level throttles).
- Monitoring hooks and an on-call escalation contact.
- A soft rollback policy to a canary subset if we observe >3% request error rate.

I've attached a snippet of the pool config we suggest for Acuity's request profile (quantized instance sizes, queue soft cap = 1024).

—Lukas

Two asks to finalize today:
1) Please confirm the exact SLA variance language we should add to the MAP: we want phrasing like "Temporary queueing variance: during the onboarding window Redwood may introduce request queueing for affected routes with up to 2s additional tail latency; requests will not be intentionally dropped unless explicitly configured by Acuity."
2) If queueing exceeds the 2s bound, what credit model kicks in (how is the credit calculated: per-minute, per-day, or lump sum % of monthly commitment)?

If we can get the wording and credit approach, Procurement will attach it to the SOW and we can sign off.

—Ryan

Subject: Escalation: approval needed for SLA variance language and credit model (AcuityAI)

Vivek — looping you in to approve the proposed temporary SLA variance and the credit approach for Acuity's onboarding window. Summary: prospect AcuityAI (deal ACU-8893) requests a 72-hour onboarding window where we allow queueing up to 2s of added tail latency on specified routes rather than shedding. Lukas confirms feasibility and suggests queue soft cap config.

Options for credit model:
- Option A (per-minute): for any minute where the measured tail latency exceeds 2s on the affected routes, credit X% of per-minute reserved capacity (needs finance input).
- Option B (daily bucket): If daily SLA target is missed for the affected routes, issue a one-time credit equal to Y% of daily committed charge.
- Option C (lump sum): Agree a fixed small credit (e.g., one week's prorated reserved fee) if the variance is breached more than once.

My recommendation: go with Option B as a predictable customer-facing approach for short onboarding windows. Marissa — can you coordinate with Finance/legal to get a template amount we can plug in (we usually use 10% daily cap for similar short variances but want to confirm).

Ryan — for transparency we'll draft the exact MAP language and the credit table and share a doc link by end of day tomorrow. If you need contract-level binding, Marissa will confirm whether a signable addendum is required or if the SOW language is sufficient.

Thanks — Tessa
